passage: I was on the same project team and watched Vasudha do something clever. Before Monday's meeting she messaged us: "Please write down any worries and drop them in the shared sheet by tonight, no names needed." Arnab, who usually talks first and fastest, said it was a waste of time. But most of us did it. On Monday, when the sheet was projected, seven of the ten worries were about the same delivery date. Arnab read them, went quiet, then said, "Okay, that is a real problem." Jiya, a first-year intern who never speaks in meetings, whispered to me, "I wrote the third one." I could not tell whether Arnab was annoyed, but he changed the schedule.

qa.q: How many of the ten worries were about the same delivery date?
qa.a: Seven of the ten worries were about the same delivery date.

qa.q: What might Jiya be feeling when whispering "I wrote the third one"?
qa.a: Jiya probably feels proud and relieved that a worry got heard, since speaking aloud in meetings is hard and writing it down felt safe.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha's suggestion help quieter people, and what might strengthen it further?
qa.a: Collecting worries privately before the group mood formed let quiet voices be heard; the team could also start meetings by reading the sheet out before anyone comments.

qa.q: What might the meeting have been like for Arnab, who usually talks first?
qa.a: Arnab may have felt surprised or uncomfortable at first, but reading the sheet and changing the schedule suggests he accepted the evidence.

grounding: A team member suggests everyone note their concerns privately before the meeting, so quiet voices are not drowned out.

passage: Tuesday. The final-year project group was about to vote on the demo plan. Nitin, the team lead, said it would be a shame to argue, so nobody argued. Sonali had a doubt about the battery but did not say it. Friday. The doubt still nagged, so Sonali asked everyone to write concerns on paper before Monday's talk. Nitin sighed but agreed. Monday. Six slips lay on the table. Four mentioned the battery. Nitin read them aloud and said, "I would not have heard this if we had just discussed." The group tested the battery that week. Sonali quietly kept the slips in a folder.

qa.q: How many of the six slips mentioned the battery?
qa.a: Four of the six slips mentioned the battery.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling on Tuesday and again on Friday?
qa.a: Sonali felt uneasy, with a doubt that was held back on Tuesday and that kept nagging by Friday, until the worry was strong enough to act on.

qa.q: What did Sonali change between Tuesday and Monday that made a difference?
qa.a: Sonali asked everyone to write concerns on paper before the talk, so views were collected before the group's mood formed.

qa.q: How might Nitin have felt while reading the slips aloud?
qa.a: Nitin may have felt surprised and a little humbled; saying "I would not have heard this" in a plain discussion shows the written slips proved their worth.

grounding: A team member suggests everyone note their concerns privately before the meeting, which keeps quiet voices from being drowned out.
